body:
in Art |   	October 5th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Here’s some rare footage of the great Mex­i­can painters Diego Rivera and Fri­da Kahlo pay­ing a vis­it to exiled Sovi­et rev­o­lu­tion­ary Leon Trot­sky and his wife, Natalia Sedo­va, in Coyoacán, Mex­i­co, in 1938.
The Trot­skys had arrived the year before, after Rivera peti­tioned the gov­ern­ment of Pres­i­dent Lázaro Cár­de­nas to grant the con­tro­ver­sial Marx­ist leader and the­o­rist sanc­tu­ary in Mex­i­co. When the Trot­skys arrived on a Nor­we­gian oil tanker at the port city of Tampi­co in Jan­u­ary of 1937, Rivera was not well, but Kahlo board­ed the ship to wel­come the Trot­skys and accom­pa­nied them on an armored train to Mex­i­co City. She invit­ed the Trot­skys to stay at her fam­i­ly home, La Casa Azul (the Blue House) in Coyoacán, now a sec­tion of Mex­i­co City. By the time this footage was tak­en by a vis­it­ing Amer­i­can named Ivan Heisler, Trot­sky and Kahlo had either had, or were about to have, a brief affair, and the friend­ship between the two cou­ples would soon fall apart. In ear­ly 1939 Trot­sky moved to anoth­er house in the same neigh­bor­hood, where he was assas­si­nat­ed in August of 1940.
If you would like to sup­port the mis­sion of Open Cul­ture, con­sid­er mak­ing a dona­tion to our site. It’s hard to rely 100% on ads, and your con­tri­bu­tions will help us con­tin­ue pro­vid­ing the best free cul­tur­al and edu­ca­tion­al mate­ri­als to learn­ers every­where. You can con­tribute through Pay­Pal, Patre­on, and Ven­mo (@openculture). Thanks!
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2013.

title: 300 Years Before ChatGPT, Jonathan Swift’s Gulliver’s Travels Imagined Machines Writing Books and Producing Knowledge (1726)
description: The print­ing press was invent­ed in the mid­dle of the fif­teenth cen­tu­ry, and it’s been down­hill for the writ­ten word ever since. Even befo
body:
The print­ing press was invent­ed in the mid­dle of the fif­teenth cen­tu­ry, and it’s been down­hill for the writ­ten word ever since. Even before then, argu­ments that the vol­ume of writ­ing being done far out­stripped the val­ue of that writ­ing sure­ly weren’t unheard of. What­ev­er the era, the most inci­sive remarks on the appar­ent vic­to­ry of ver­bal quan­ti­ty over ver­bal qual­i­ty tend to have come from writ­ers them­selves. No less a satirist than Jonathan Swift made it one of his many tar­gets in Gul­liv­er’s Trav­els (1726), imag­in­ing an elab­o­rate machine of wood and wire called “the Engine” (see illus­tra­tion above) that auto­mat­i­cal­ly gen­er­ates text, though few remem­ber it — or rather, few remem­bered it until the rise of large lan­guage mod­els in the real world.
Gul­liv­er encoun­ters that tech­no­log­i­cal mar­vel, the Engine, at an insti­tu­tion called the Acad­e­my of Pro­jec­tors in the city of Laga­do. Swift’s pro­tag­o­nist records its cre­ator’s expla­na­tion as fol­lows: “Every one knew how labo­ri­ous the usu­al method is of attain­ing to arts and sci­ences; where­as, by his con­trivance, the most igno­rant per­son, at a rea­son­able charge, and with a lit­tle bod­i­ly labor, might write books in phi­los­o­phy, poet­ry, pol­i­tics, laws, math­e­mat­ics, and the­ol­o­gy, with­out the least assis­tance from genius or study.” The Engine’s oper­a­tion, with its unwieldy, clack­ing com­po­nents and a scram­bling staff of young crankers, read­ers, and scribes, may strike us as bizarre, just as it did audi­ences in the eigh­teenth cen­tu­ry. But in our time, when stu­dents can write their papers lit­er­al­ly with­out giv­ing it a thought (to say noth­ing of what their pro­fes­sors may be get­ting up to), its con­cept now sounds all too plau­si­ble.
“This is one of the ear­li­est known men­tions of a machine that could be con­sid­ered as a com­put­er in lit­er­a­ture, more than a hun­dred years pri­or to the first cal­cu­lat­ing engine designs by Charles Bab­bage,” writes Chris Gar­cia at the web site of the Com­put­er His­to­ry Muse­um. “The Engine might be seen as a com­put­er, but per­haps it’s bet­ter thought of as a sort of ran­dom-num­ber gen­er­a­tor,” spout­ing out whichev­er words of the local lan­guage that cor­re­spond with the dig­its. That post dates from ten years, near­ly to the day, before the launch of Chat­G­PT, which changed the gen­er­al pub­lic’s ideas about what com­put­ers can and can’t do. We may dis­agree about whether a machine can tru­ly gen­er­ate “a com­plete body of all arts and sci­ences,” as the Engine’s inven­tor intends, but it no longer sounds like sheer­est fan­ta­sy.
Swift had in mind not engi­neers of arti­fi­cial intel­li­gence but the Roy­al Soci­ety, whose enthu­si­asm for sci­en­tif­ic knowl­edge and exper­i­men­ta­tion he saw as insuf­fi­cient­ly teth­ered to real­i­ty, or at least prac­ti­cal­i­ty. In addi­tion to the Engine, writes lit­er­a­ture pro­fes­sor Robin Bates, “Swift imag­ines sci­en­tists attempt­ing to extract sun­beams from cucum­bers, soft­en mar­ble into pil­lows and pin­cush­ions, replace silk­worms with spi­ders (and hav­ing them eat bright­ly col­ored flies so the threads will be pre-dyed), mix paint by smell, reassem­ble orig­i­nal food stuffs from excre­ment, and build hous­es from the top down (in imi­ta­tion of the bee and the spi­der).” His satire holds up today thanks to his under­stand­ing that, “for all the promis­es of the Enlight­en­ment, the Age of Rea­son, and the Sci­en­tif­ic and Tech­no­log­i­cal Rev­o­lu­tions,” our attempts to change the world “founder the moment we start ignor­ing human nature.” But who needs human nature, the Pro­jec­tors of today might argue, when you’ve got enough com­pute?
Relat­ed con­tent:
How George Orwell Pre­dict­ed the Rise of “AI Slop” in Nine­teen Eighty-Four (1949)
When Roald Dahl Wrote a Sto­ry Pre­dict­ing the Rise of Chat­G­PT and Oth­er AI Large Lan­guage Mod­els (1954)
Sci-Fi Writer Arthur C. Clarke Pre­dict­ed the Rise of Arti­fi­cial Intel­li­gence & the Exis­ten­tial Ques­tions We Would Need to Answer (1978)
Why AI Com­pa­nies Are Buy­ing — And Then Destroy­ing — Old Books
George Orwell Got a B- at Har­vard, When Michael Crich­ton Sub­mit­ted an Orwell Essay as His Own

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

Daily Newsletter
                Hrag Vartanian on Mala Iqbal's vignettes of the metropolis, museum union updates, and Mamdani doubles art grants. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Detail of Mala Iqbal, “Transparent Friend” (2025)
    
        
            It’s a lovely day for upholding labor rights. As Whitney Museum of American Art workers celebrate a new contract, Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar brings us a hopeful update from unions at three other institutions: the American Folk Art Museum, Brooklyn Museum, and the Guggenheim. What better reminder of why we fight for culture than a show of beautiful new paintings? Hyperallergic Editor-at-Large Hrag Vartanian writes movingly about Mala Iqbal's vignettes of the metropolis and its familiar strangers, on view at JJ Murphy in Manhattan.It’s also Banned Books Week, when we defend freedom of expression even more vociferously than usual. If you’re in NYC, head to the Brooklyn Public Library for a timely talk with artist and author Christopher Myers, film producer Karin Chien, and publisher Namrata Tripathi, moderated by Vartanian.—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

	
		
		Mala Iqbal Paints the Space We Share With Strangers
		
	
	
		Figures jostle the surface of every Mala Iqbal canvas with the energy of a great metropolis. Many are bathed in an orange and yellow glow, a tinge of artifice for people who live under electric light, places where even the sun isn’t enough. Some of the paintings forgo that effect, like “Through the Curtains” (2026). Left to right, we see a scene of collapse, which is obscured by a tulle curtain rendering like a faded negative; a figure reacts, almost numbly; and ultimately another curtain finishes the scene with a pictograph-like pattern — life, transformed by a screen, experienced by someone, and turned into an indecipherable language. I view it as a metaphor for how our screens deliver collapse and violence with every scroll, faster than we can process it. | Hrag Vartanian
	
	
		Read More
	


                    
                    
                    
                        Surveying Hank Willis Thomas's most iconic artworks across a range of media, this exhibition at Zimmerli Art Museum explores how images shape perception, identity, and values. By questioning what feels familiar, the artist connects historical moments of resistance to our lives today and invites us to remain open to change. 
                        
                            Learn more

Guggenheim Museum, and American Folk Art Museum ratify their contracts.NYC artists can now receive up to $10,000 in city-funded grants, double the amount of previous appropriations, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs announce.The British Museum will provide audio tour options for its Bayeux Tapestry exhibition after a blind patron pursued legal action against the London institution last week.Francis Lee Rogers, a 63-year-old artist whose neighbors and subjects were the birds of Central Park, is found dead.Pocket Review

An Exhibition Devoted to Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock Argues for Krasner’s Equal Significance
		
									
	October 5, 2026 5:00am	
					
							
		
			
				

			
			
			
	
			
					Lee Krasner at her home in East Hampton, New York, August 1953
									Tony Vaccaro/Hulton Archive/Getty Images.
	


				

	Lee Krasner’s art has always been tough to is tough to define, because she was constantly changing and reinventing her work. Unlike her fellow Abstract Expressionists, whose paintings could be easily recognized by certain characteristics, Krasner worked in cycles.

	“Krasner refused to become a serial painter with a repeated trademark format,” wrote art historian Barbara Rose in the catalog for Krasner’s 1983 traveling retrospective, which opened at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston. “A painting by Krasner is recognized by its style, its rhythm, its mastery of color and nuance, its fine detail, and its floral, naturalistic, or organic imagery.”

	Krasner was also hard for art historians to assess because she was self-effacing and bad about documenting her work (which she sometimes destroyed). And she reputedly had a prickly personality, alienating major critics. Add all this to the fact that for many years she was known mainly as the wife and then the widow of Jackson Pollock, and it’s no wonder that Krasner’s recognition came late in the game.

	Toward the end of her life, and in the decades since, Krasner has been celebrated for her organic, calligraphic forms, strong colors, and rhythmic lines. Now, an exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art titled “Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous” will showcase her paintings alongside works by Pollock, celebrating them as “artistic peers and life partners.” The Met was the site of Krasner’s memorial service in 1984; now, more than 40 years later, it is fitting that it’s the venue for this major two-artist show.


			
			
	Early life and artistic beginnings
			
										
					Image Credit: Copyright © Museum of Modern Art, New York.				
					
				

	Born in Brooklyn in October 1908, Lena Krassner was the first in her family to begin life in the United States. Her parents, Joseph and Anna, had emigrated from a small village near Odessa to escape antisemitic persecution and start a new life.

	The Krassners were an Orthodox Jewish family who spoke a combination of Russian, Yiddish, and English and valued culture and education. They owned a small produce store in Brooklyn, run mostly by Anna. Krasner later said that she was raised to be independent and that as long as she didn’t make financial demands of her parents, she was free to study art.

	Which is what she did, as soon as she could. When Krasner was just 13 years old, she enrolled at Washington Irving High School in Manhattan—the only school in New York then with an art program for girls. It meant commuting from Brooklyn to Manhattan, but Krasner could major in studio art. After graduating from high school, she was awarded a scholarship to the Women’s Art School at Cooper Union, which trained women to be teachers (a fallback career option that Krasner never used).

	Krasner’s three-year program at Cooper Union was just part of what made her one of the most extensively trained New York School artists. She also took classes at the Art Students League and continued on to the prestigious National Academy of Design for an additional three years. While there, she studied life drawing, and some of her earliest extant works are drawings she made from the academy’s plaster casts.

	Despite this traditional training, Krasner’s preferences lay elsewhere. Two of her National Academy classmates remembered her as a “talented, forceful redhead who was always trying to drag her fellow students to modern art exhibitions.” When the Museum of Modern Art opened, in 1929, she went immediately. “I’d seen my first Matisse, my first Picasso, my first Braque, and it was like a bomb that exploded,” she explained in a 1964 interview. Matisse, in particular, remained one of the artist’s personal favorites throughout her career.

		
			
			
	1930s and early 1940s
			
										
					Image Credit: Collection of the Columbus Museum, Georgia. Artwork copyright © The Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York.				
					
				

	As a young artist in her twenties, Krasner supported herself by making illustrations and waitressing at a nightclub called Sam Johnson’s in Greenwich Village, the neighborhood where she lived. At this bohemian spot she met and befriended several art world figures, including a young Harold Rosenberg (later the New Yorker art critic) and an equally young Clement Greenberg.

	It was around this time that she started calling herself Lee and altered the spelling of her last name. She also joined the mural division of the Works Progress Administration Federal Art Project in 1935, its inaugural year, and was in charge of enlarging other artists’ mural sketches to full size (something that prepared her for the scale of her later monumental works).

	In 1937, in parallel with her WPA day job, Krasner took night classes with painter and influential teacher Hans Hofmann, who recognized her talent and offered her a partial scholarship. Over the three years she studied with him, she was exposed to Cubism and drew from nature—whether from a nude model or a still life. She was also privy to Hofmann’s infectious love of painting and his dedication to it, despite his backhanded compliment that remained with her for the rest of her life. “I can remember very clearly his criticism one day when he came in and said about the painting up in front of him, ‘This is so good you would not believe it was done by a woman,’” Krasner later recalled. “Well, that’s pretty difficult to understand.”

	Krasner joined the American Abstract Artists and participated in three of their shows in the early 1940s, exhibiting mostly Cubist still lifes in gray monochromes. At AAA she met like-minded artists, including Piet Mondrian, who had by then moved to New York. (Mondrian and Krasner both loved to boogie-woogie, apparently, and sometimes went dancing together.) Unlike Hofmann, Mondrian gave Krasner a compliment that strengthened her resolve. “Very strong inner rhythm,” he told her upon seeing one of her paintings at an AAA exhibition. “Stay with it.”

		
			
			
	“Something blew” with Jackson Pollock
			
										
					Image Credit: Private collection. Artwork copyright © The Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York.				
					
				

	Krasner had already begun making a name for herself when she was included as one of three emerging American artists in a 1942 exhibition of American and French paintings organized by another mentor, the modernist John Graham. The other two in the exhibit were Willem de Kooning (whom she knew) and Jackson Pollock (whom she didn’t). Krasner heard from a friend that Pollock was a good painter, and after realizing that they lived only a block from each other, she went to his studio to meet him. “A bomb exploded when I saw that first French show [at MoMA]. The next bomb that exploded was this incident when I walked into his studio,” Krasner later said. “There were five or six canvases around, and they had the same impact on me. Something blew.”

	The two artists became romantically involved soon after, with Krasner starting to share Pollock’s studio on 8th Street. Krasner kept working, but it was one of her least fruitful periods; for Pollock, on the other hand, it was highly productive. It was during this time that she made a major transition from working with a visual model, as Hofmann had taught her, to starting with a blank canvas and her own imagination to create nonobjective images.

	“Jackson always treated me as an artist,” said Krasner. “I was a painter before I knew him, and he knew that, and when we were together, I couldn’t have stayed with him one day if he didn’t treat me as a painter.”

		
			
			
	Mid- to late 1940s
			
										
					Image Credit: Collection of the Philadelphia Museum of Art. Artwork copyright © 2026 The Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York.				
					
				

	The couple married in October 1945 and moved from Greenwich Village to East Hampton the next month. They asked art collector Peggy Guggenheim (whose Art of This Century gallery Pollock had joined in 1943) to be a witness at their wedding, but she declined because she had a luncheon date; a $2,000 loan from her did help the pair buy the clapboard farmhouse that they made home on Fireplace Road in the hamlet of Springs.

	Much more isolated than they were while living in New York City, the two focused on their work. Pollock started painting in an upstairs bedroom but then moved his studio to the spacious barn that they had renovated. Krasner then used that upstairs room as her studio, working mostly on small easel paintings there.

	She started making what she called her “Little Image” paintings, with dense surfaces full of small symbols arranged in grid formats. In the winter of 1947, when it was too cold for Krasner to paint in the bedroom studio, Pollock suggested she make a mosaic downstairs near the stove, using cut colored glass that was left over from his WPA work. She used two old wagon wheels they had cleared from the barn as the base and filled them with tesserae, broken glass bottles she’d collected, coins, jewelry, and personal items. Mixing mediums was a preparation of sorts for the collage paintings she would start making soon after, and the gridded mosaic format may have influenced her “Little Images” paintings.

		
			
			
	1950s
			
										
					Image Credit: ASOM Collection. Artwork copyright © 2026 The Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists
Rights Society (ARS), New York.				
					
				

	In the 1950s Krasner began making colorful collages, destroying her older drawings and canvases and reworking them into new pieces. It started when she was looking over drawings for an exhibition and, dissatisfied with some of them, tore them up. When she saw the possibilities in the pile of ripped up drawings, she started collaging.

	For the first few years after marrying Pollock and moving out to East Hampton, Krasner barely exhibited. She had her first-ever solo show in the fall of 1951 at Betty Parsons Gallery. Her next came a few years later, in 1955 at Stable Gallery.

	By 1956, Pollock’s alcoholism had worsened and he started a public affair with painter Ruth Kligman. Friends in Europe invited Krasner to visit, and since she’d never been abroad, she took them up on their offer. While in France, she received a phone call from Clement Greenberg informing her that Pollock had been killed in a car crash.

		
			
			
	Post-Pollock productivity
			
										
					Image Credit: Collection of the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York. Artwork copyright © The Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York.				
					
				

	Krasner returned to East Hampton, and a year after Pollock’s death, she moved her studio into the barn, which allowed her to work on a bigger scale. This period marked the “final liberation of Krasner’s art,” according to curator and critic William Rubin, although Pollock’s fame continued to impede reception of her art even after his death.

	She had a solo show at Martha Jackson Gallery in 1958, her third New York solo presentation in seven years (incidentally, all were at galleries owned by women). The paintings she exhibited in 1958 were large canvases with thinly applied paint in big, curvilinear shapes. “The question came up whether one would continue painting,” Krasner said about persevering after Pollock’s tragic accident. “I guess this was my answer.”

	Krasner suffered another loss the following year: the death of her mother. She developed insomnia and started working at night, using a limited color palette of umber tones because she was painting under artificial light and preferred natural light when using color. A friend, poet Richard Howard, dubbed these her “Night Journeys.” When she overcame her insomnia, the color came back; she created brightly colored works she called her “Primary Series.”

	This stage of Krasner’s career, after Pollock’s death, was one of her most productive, even though she was simultaneously managing Pollock’s estate and promoting his legacy (a role in which she had a reputation for being a tough negotiator).

		
			
			
	Late recognition
			
										
					Image Credit: Collection of the National Gallery of Victoria, Melbourne, Australia. Artwork copyright © 2026 The Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York.				
					
				

	Toward the end of her life, Krasner received belated recognition, thanks in part to the second-wave feminism of the 1970s. She had major retrospectives in her lifetime, beginning with one at London’s Whitechapel Gallery in 1965. This was a turning point for Krasner, who was finally starting to be considered on her own merits, and not just as Pollock’s widow. But it was a slow process. “Even today it’s difficult for people to see me, or to speak to me, or observe my work, and not connect it with Pollock. They cannot free themselves,” Krasner said in a 1972 interview, in regard to why she had not yet had a retrospective in the United States. “So this may be one of the reasons I’ve not been offered a show. I wouldn’t know if there are others.”

	The following year, in 1973, she had her first American retrospective at the Whitney Museum of American Art—a significant milestone. Curator Marcia Tucker wrote in the accompanying catalog: “Today, Lee Krasner is considered a prototype by many younger painters. She is encouraging and generous, tough and strong-willed, gregarious and adventurous, full of anecdotes and ideas. Most important, the enthusiasm for her work continues to grow as the contributions she has made are being fully realized.”

	Krasner’s next American retrospective, which began at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, and then traveled to New York’s Museum of Modern Art, opened in 1983 on the artist’s 75th birthday. It was still on view when she died, in June 1984, at New York Hospital.

	A few months later, a memorial service was held for her in the Medieval Sculpture Court at the Met. At the service, Time magazine art critic Robert Hughes dubbed her the “Mother Courage of Abstract Expressionism.”


			
			
			
	
			
					Lee Krasner next to her work Rising Green, November 2, 1973
									Newsday RM via Getty Images.

title: What Changing Views of the Young British Artists Say About the Art World Today
description: In his latest bestseller, London Falling, Patrick Radden Keefe refers to art in his prologue to illustrate the way the city of London changed near t
body:
In his latest bestseller, London Falling, Patrick Radden Keefe refers to art in his prologue to illustrate the way the city of London changed near the end of the 20th century: In 1988, a group of young artists used a derelict warehouse in the docklands of southeast London as the venue for their first group exhibition, “Freeze.” He doesn’t say anything else, assuming the reader will know who those artists became: the Young British Artists, or YBAs.

	Arguably Britain’s most famous artistic group ever, the YBAs were a symptom of their moment. They rocketed to fame in the early ’90s, as London was undergoing a profound renaissance—or rupture, depending on how you look back on it now. Their legacy has ebbed and flowed in parallel with Britain’s national image, peaking in the heady atmosphere of the end of the millennium and gaining nuance as it has fallen ever since. And that legacy has continued to be reexamined in notable exhibitions, among them shows for Tracey Emin at Tate Modern earlier this year, Jenny Saville at London’s National Portrait Gallery in 2025, and Sarah Lucas at Tate Britain in 2023—as well as “The 90s: Art and Fashion,” an exhibition devoted to the art and pop culture of the YBA decade opening at Tate Britain in October.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Making a definite list of who is an “official” YBA is difficult. The designation is sometimes reserved for the artists included in the original “Freeze” exhibition, while other times it applies to those in collector Charles Saatchi’s “Young British Artists” exhibitions from 1992 to 1995, and still other times to the artist list for the Royal Academy’s 1997 “Sensation” show. Many, but not all, of the members in the orbit of Damien Hirst graduated from Goldsmiths in the late 1980s and early ’90s, and there are dozens of other exhibitions that pulled together different arrangements of artists. Then there are the questions of who was friends with who or might be dating, and of course what the media made of it all at the time. With that said, the key YBAs are definitely Hirst, Emin, Lucas, Saville, Marc Quinn, the Chapman Brothers, Gary Hume, Michael Landy, Gillian Wearing, Chris Ofili, Angus Fairhurst, Rachel Whiteread, and Anya Gallaccio.
	

	When “Freeze” opened in its East End warehouse in 1988, it was a scene. In his memoir about being a YBA groupie, Lucky Kunst, critic and curator Gregor Muir described the way the exhibition marked the start of a new culture of packed openings and the feeling of a real community of artists and art people who went to all of them, drank and drugged excessively, and knew each other well. Genuine friendship between the artists was the glue that held the group together, more than any guiding aesthetic qualities or artistic questions in search of answers. If pressed, one could say that YBA artists shared a desire to shock. But whether through revulsion, violence, sex, or strange new ways of using space or materials, the artists in the YBA set sought reactions from viewers—with good or bad mattering less than the intensity of the reaction itself.

	IN 1992, THE BRITISH-IRAQI ad man andcollector Charles Saatchi hosted the first “Young British Artists” exhibition at his gallery near Sloane Square in West London, the first time the moniker was officially enlisted. The exhibition debuted Hirst’s infamous shark in a formaldehyde tank, with the title The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living (1991). Around the same time, three more defining YBA works were exhibited elsewhere in London: Marc Quinn’s Self (1991), a sculpture of his own head made with eight pints of his own frozen blood; Sarah Lucas’s Two Fried Eggs and a Kebab (1992), a table on which the foods in the title were arranged to suggest a set of breasts and a vagina; and Rachel Whiteread’s Ghost (1990), a plaster cast of an entire room of an abandoned Victorian house. These four works, along with Tracey Emin’s My Bed (1998), stunned the international art world and have defined the YBA image and legacy ever since. I would wager that many readers can picture some or all of them right now—they have become genuinely iconic.
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Damien Hirst: The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living, 1991, on view in an exhibition at Tate Modern, London, in 2012. 
									hoto Oli Scarff/Getty Images
	



	The YBAs were the beneficiaries—or maybe victims—of superb branding. Saatchi, whose advertising firm Saatchi & Saatchi was most famous for masterminding the brand strategy of Margaret Thatcher’s final two election campaigns, purchased a huge volume of work directly from the artists who would become known as the YBAs, including the works mentioned above. While the amounts he paid were not negligible by the metrics of the time (he bought Quinn’s Self for £13,000 in 1991 and Emin’s My Bed for £150,000 in 2000, for example), he resold the works with a mark-up of over 1,000 percent (he sold Self in 2005 for approximately £1.5 million and My Bed in 2014 for about £2.5 million).

	In 1997, the Royal Academy hosted a blockbuster exhibition of works in Saatchi’s collection, titled “Sensation,” that broke visitor records and also garnered significant criticism for basically being a preliminary saleroom for one man’s collection. Saatchi was unprecedented in London—no collectors of his wealth and strategic mindset were buying in the city at the time. He had more or less free rein to buy anything he wanted, and to manufacture a frenzy around the artists he collected to make his investments so lucrative. After all, he was an ad man.
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Jake and Dinos Chapman: Zygotic Acceleration, Biogenetic, De-Sublimated Libidinal Model, 1995; on view in “Sensation” at the Brooklyn Museum, 1999–2000.
									hoto Susan Watts/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images
	



	By 1998, the year after “Sensation,” the Observer writer Andrew Anthony wrote in an article titled “Why Be a YBA?” that “increasingly, the artists and the surrounding world of dealers, gallerists, hangers-on, [and] parties have become more ‘interesting’ than their art.” The line between them, he noted, “had already been blurred,” but by the turn of the millennium it had fully been erased. Throughout the decade from “Freeze” in 1988 to this moment of flux in 1998, the YBAs’ relationship to the “establishment” had been paradoxical. They promoted themselves as disrupters who had come from outside the art world to shake things up. But they were graduates of prestigious art schools who were in with major dealers and collectors within a few years of graduation: chiefly Saatchi and Jay Jopling, the Old Etonian son of a member of Thatcher’s cabinet who founded the gallery White Cube. They exhibited in major museum exhibitions around Europe and North America, and while those shows did garner some controversy (the Clintons and Rudy Giuliani agreed that the Brooklyn Museum’s iteration of “Sensation” was deeply offensive), they were also huge platforms that conferred institutional legitimacy.
	

	The media personas of some of the YBAs, most famously Emin, pulled in the other direction. Emin was famous for appearing drunk on television, throwing drug-fueled multi-day benders, and being brazenly promiscuous, working class, and generally unfazed by anyone’s expectation that she be anything but herself. Her behavior epitomized the fuck-it attitude of her YBA peers. But she, too, became the establishment: first by being a punk celebrity, which made her a household name, and eventually by sticking around long enough and commanding high enough prices at auction to win mainstream acceptance culminating in her blockbuster Tate Modern show this year.

	IT’S NO ACCIDENT that the YBAs gettingthe most attention now, both in museums and on the art market, are women. Saville’s 1992 painting Propped sold for over £9 million in 2018, breaking records for the most expensive work ever sold by a female living artist at the time. Emin’s commercially minded paintings and neon works do what they’re meant to: Several of her post-cancer canvases have sold for seven figures, although none has beaten the £2.5 million record set by My Bed in 2014. Some of the YBAs never made eminently sellable paintings but have still grown into respected art world fixtures as they continue making installations or transient work. Rachel Whiteread’s sculptural practice has always had a quiet, stable monumentality, and it continues to stand the test of time. Anya Gallaccio’s interest in decay and mortality pivoted nicely into a tactful, timely engagement with eco-consciousness and connection to place.
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Rachel Whiteread’s installation Untitled (100 Spaces),1995, in “Sensation” at the Brooklyn Museum.  
									hoto Susan Watts/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images
	



	Many of the male YBAs have evolved rather less, and their desire to offend in order to provoke no longer holds the inciting power it once did. For example, Tom Whyman pointed out when writing about an online furor over the Chapman Brothers for ArtReview in 2023 that they are too big to cancel, because for their collectors “any such ‘cancellation’ would negatively impact their investment.” Hirst’s work now rivals that of Jeff Koons in seeming specifically conceived for asset-class collectors. His truly heinous series of sculptures “Treasures from the Wreck of the Unbelievable” premiered in 2017 at the Pinault Collection’s Palazzo Grassi and Punta della Dogana in Venice before being allocated to other collectors in editions of multiples of various works, which he said earned him a final total of $330 million. I saw some of them installed at Rome’s Galleria Borghese in 2021 and found them utterly foul—and comically empty when seen alongside the complexity of Bernini’s work. When the image of the artist transcends his art, it might result in good sales, but it doesn’t make the art meaningful.

	“I GOT LUCKY AT WHITE CUBE,” reads a T-shirt currently for sale from Plaster, a London-based art brand run by Milo Astaire and Finn Constantine (once just a magazine, now a physical shop, event space, and creator of content). The shirt could have just as easily been sold in 1995, when Jay Jopling was hawking Hirsts from his first gallery location in St. James, with openings that overflowed into the street and what one imagines was a fine white dusting of cocaine covering the loos. It mimics the shirts that Sarah Lucas and Tracey Emin sold out of The Shop, the space they opened in the East End in 1993, with slogans like “Have you wanked over me yet” and “I’m so fucky” drawn in black marker. Though it was only open for six months, The Shop epitomized the genuine energy of the YBAs when they were just starting out: goofy, for sale, and always keen to hang out. “Lots of people now say they went to The Shop when they didn’t, but we know exactly who did because we were there every day,” Emin said years later.
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Sarah Lucas and Tracey Emin in front of The Shop in London’s East End, 1993.
									©Pauline Daly/Courtesy Pauline Daly and Sadie Coles HQ, London
	



	After the peak of fame and power with the Royal Academy exhibition in 1997, which toured to the Hamburger Bahnhof in Berlin and the Brooklyn Museum of Art, there was a dearth of interest in the YBAs for a decade or so. But when the Olympics came to London in 2012, bringing with them a very un-British wave of nostalgia and civic pride, interest revived and exhibitions were staged around the city to celebrate the legacy of the early days of the group. Since then, big-name YBAs have mostly found platforms in solo retrospectives and other shows, like Tate Britain’s forthcoming “The 90s: Art and Fashion,” that offer new looks back to the YBA decade.

	While British art has always suffered from an air of provinciality, the YBAs seemed poised to change that when they put Britain on the proverbial map of contemporary art in a way it had never been before. But British art, like Britain itself, continues to suffer something of an identity complex. The YBA legacy has traced the rise and fall of perceptions of Britain itself, both at home and abroad. Stepping into the spotlight alongside Tony Blair’s New Labour, Kate Moss, Vivienne Westwood, and the Beckhams, the energy around YBAs in the ’90s epitomized Cool Britannia. But the fashionable-at-the-time nakedness of the YBAs’ desire for money, most completely embodied by Hirst, quickly became crass.
	


			
			
			
	
			
									Tate Photography
	



	Though the conventional story told about the YBAs is one of friendship and community, what stands out now is their allegiance to neoliberal individualism. The flashy, shocking work that made the group seem invincible ended up making it banal, appearing now to be little more than branding. And Britain itself, after the financial and cultural boom of the ’90s, has in the post-recession era settled into its new role as butler to the world, to borrow a phrase from writer and money-laundering muckraker Oliver Bullough.

	The stiff-upper-lip self-deprecation that now leads your average Londoner to say that Britain is shit embodies a malaise that makes the optimism of Cool Britannia feel very far away indeed. With hindsight, it’s obvious that the YBA moment was defined by a Faustian sale of the self to the highest bidder that encapsulates the intensifying symbiosis of the market and art itself. It is a soulless ethos for artmaking, but one that continues to echo through the global art ecosystem.
